<ConflictType> — Evidence shows both potential harms and benefits, with no consensus on overall harm

Research clusters into two incompatible narratives: one emphasizes risks for vulnerable subgroups and excessive use [d1,d2,d5,d6], while the other highlights cognitive, emotional, and therapeutic benefits and minimal harm for most children [d1,d2,d8]. Some sources explicitly argue violent games do not create violent children [d7], and others document curvilinear effects where moderate use is associated with better outcomes than non-use [d2].

</think>
The evidence presents two incompatible perspectives on whether video games are harmful to children’s mental health. One body of research links excessive or violent gaming to increased aggression in some children, sleep and social problems, and even extreme harms in unsupervised contexts [d5,d6,d4]. Another set of studies and expert reviews reports cognitive and emotional benefits, improved mood, resilience, and therapeutic uses, with harm concentrated in a small minority of vulnerable children [d1,d2,d8]. A contrary view asserts that violent games do not create violent children and that other factors drive aggression [d7].

Given these conflicting findings, there is no single consensus that video games are uniformly harmful or harmless to all children’s mental health [d1,d2,d5,d8].
